analysis_steps.goal: Create CO moment maps and position-velocity diagrams

method.value: Masked moment technique: smooth a copy of the cleaned cube spatially with a Gaussian (FWHM = 1.5x synthesized beam) and in velocity with Hanning smoothing, apply a 0.9 sigma flux-density threshold to create a 3D mask, and compute moments 0, 1, and 2 from the un-smoothed cubes within the mask; extract PVDs along slits A, B, and C

evidence.quote: In short, in this technique, a copy of the cleaned data cube is first Gaussian-smoothed spatially (with a FWHM that is $1.5x$ that of the synthesised beam) and then Hanning-smoothed in velocity.

Further support to the presence of disturbed/non-circular kinematic components comes from the analysis of the CO position-velocity diagrams (PVDs) extracted along different PAs and illustrated in Figures 8 and 9.

findings_qualitative.value: I00183 likely formed through a major prograde merger between two gas-rich spiral galaxies no older than ~2 Gyr, evidenced by prominent tidal tails extending up to 40 kpc.

evidence.quote: We claim that the most likely explanation for such structures is that they are tidal tails, whose characteristics lead us to conclude that I00183 probably formed through a major merger between two gas-rich spirals, characterised by a prograde encounter and no older than 2 Gyr.

findings_qualitative.value: Extreme molecular gas excitation (R_31 up to >=60, T_ex >> 50 K, optically thin) is spatially correlated with the radio lobes, indicating an ongoing jet-ISM interaction.

evidence.quote: The analysis of the $R_{\rm 31} \equiv S_{\rm CO(3-2)}/S_{\rm CO(1-0)}$ flux density ratio shows the presence of a high-excitation gas component with $R_{\rm 31}$ reaching values up to $60$ (see Section 3.4).

The spatial correlation between the regions where the largest line ratios are observed and the location of the radio lobes suggests that also in I00183 the expanding radio plasma is likely responsible for the extreme gas conditions in the circumnuclear regions.

findings_qualitative.value: The CO kinematics shows no ordered circular rotation, but contains a high-velocity non-rotational component associated with a kpc-scale molecular outflow that cannot be powered by supernovae or current AGN radiation pressure alone, pointing to frustrated radio jets or past higher AGN activity.

evidence.quote: By comparing the energetics and geometrical properties of the outflow with that of possible driving mechanisms (i.e. SNe, AGN radiation pressure, jet-induced shocks), we conclude that this may be triggered by either radiation from the AGN in the past or the kinetic energy input from a frustrated radio jet.

claims.hypothesis: I00183 formed through a recent major merger of two gas-rich spiral galaxies in a prograde encounter.
claims.experiment: Performed deep i-band VST photometry, IRAF ELLIPSE/BMODEL 2D light modelling and subtraction, and compared residual asymmetric structures with the GALMER simulation database.
claims.result: Identified prominent tidal tails extending up to ~40 kpc East and ~35 kpc South, plus Northern and Western tails in residuals, matching GALMER prograde Sa+Sb merger run #431 (<2 Gyr old) and ~10^10 M_sun of central molecular gas.
claims.finding: I00183 formed via a major prograde merger of two gas-rich spirals no older than ~2 Gyr.

evidence.quote: We claim that the most likely explanation for such structures is that they are tidal tails, whose characteristics lead us to conclude that I00183 probably formed through a major merger between two gas-rich spirals, characterised by a prograde encounter and no older than 2 Gyr.

claims.hypothesis: The two compact optical residuals in the central region (separated by ~1.1'' or ~5.2 kpc) trace close binary nuclei from the progenitor galaxies.
claims.experiment: Compared the spatial locations of the two optical compact residuals with the optical peak, VLBI radio core, CO(1-0) and CO(3-2) distributions, and 100/250 GHz ALMA continuum maps.
claims.result: Both the optical peak and radio core lie within the southern compact residual; neither CO emission nor ALMA continuum shows a double peak or morphological correlation with the northern compact residual.
claims.finding: It is unlikely that the two compact residuals trace close binary nuclei; they more plausibly arise from a nuclear dust lane.

evidence.quote: We therefore conclude that it is unlikely that the two residual point-like structures in Figure 15 trace the presence of close binary nuclei. Another hypothesis would be that both compact residuals arise from a prominent nuclear dust lane.

claims.hypothesis: Expanding small-scale radio jets are interacting with the circumnuclear ISM and altering its excitation conditions.
claims.experiment: Re-imaged ALMA CO(3-2) and CO(1-0) cubes to a common uv-range and 0.42'' x 0.32'' beam, constructed the R_31 flux density ratio map, and overlaid 2.3 GHz VLBI radio continuum contours.
claims.result: Found average R_31 ~ 10 and local values >= 60 around the SE radio jet, well above the optically thick limit of 9 and implying optically thin gas with T_ex >> 50 K and n > 3000 cm^-3.
claims.finding: Extreme molecular gas excitation around the radio lobes supports an ongoing jet-ISM interaction.

evidence.quote: Furthermore, by comparing the relative strength of the two CO transitions, we find extreme gas excitation (i.e. $T_{\rm ex}\gg50$ K) around the radio lobes, supporting the case for a jet-ISM interaction.
the gas can be overall considered as highly excited, with average $R_{\rm 31}\approx10$, reaching values $\geq60$ around the location of the SE radio jet

claims.hypothesis: The high-velocity non-circular CO kinematic component is a kpc-scale molecular outflow driven by supernovae, current AGN radiation pressure, or radio jets.
claims.experiment: Extracted PVDs, fitted 1- and 2-Gaussian models to integrated spectra with BIC testing, measured outflow mass and energetics from a 1.0'' x 0.3'' box along the outflow axis, and compared with SNe, AGN bolometric radiation pressure, and dynamical radio jet models.
claims.result: Two-Gaussian fits are strongly preferred (Delta BIC = 21.8 and 52.2), yielding V_out ~ 439 km/s, M_dot_out ~ 609 M_sun/yr (or 150 M_sun/yr with diffuse gas), P_dot_out ~ 1.2e36 g cm s^-2, and E_dot ~ 1.82e43 erg/s. SNe (68 M_sun/yr) and current AGN radiation pressure (2.06e35 g cm s^-2) fall short, while radio jet power (~10^43 erg/s) and age (14 Myr) match.
claims.finding: Supernovae and present-day AGN radiation pressure cannot alone drive the molecular outflow; it is plausibly driven by frustrated radio jets or higher AGN radiation pressure in the past.

evidence.quote: This excludes the power from supernovae as the main driver of the molecular outflow.
We thus conclude that the AGN radiation pressure is unlikely to be the only driver of the molecular outflow, at least at present times.
Hence both the energetics and timescale analysis suggest that the radio jets can plausibly drive the putative CO outflow.

why_this_data.value: High-resolution (~1 kpc) ALMA CO(1-0) and CO(3-2) observations combined with deep VST i-band imaging and VLBI data allow exploring the link between merger history, AGN/jet activity, and kpc-scale molecular outflows in a transitional ULIRG at z > 0.3, complementing 10x lower-resolution Cycle 0 ALMA data.

evidence.quote: Such multi-wavelength analysis allows us to explore the link between galaxy merger, AGN activity, radio jet expansion and galactic-scale (i.e. $\sim$kpc-scale) molecular outflows, for the first time with a high level of detail in an ULIRG at $z>0.3$.

The analysis of the multiple CO transitions presented in this paper allows us to complement the results obtained from the study at ten times lower spatial resolution (i.e. beam FWHM $= 3.10\ensuremath{''} \times 2.20\ensuremath{''}$, equivalent to $\approx 14.7 \times 10.4$ kpc) of the sole CO(1-0) transition presented in (cite: Ruffa18).

why_this_method.value: Briggs robust=0.5 gives the best trade-off between sensitivity and resolution; masked moment technique recovers flux while minimising noise; matching uv-range and beam is required for reliable line ratio maps; BIC test rigorously verifies the need for a broad second Gaussian component.

evidence.quote: In all the cases, Briggs weighting with a robust parameter of 0.5 was adopted, thus obtaining the best trade-off between sensitivity and resolution.
We also performed a BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) test (cite: Liddle07) to verify the statistical significance of one model with respect to the other.
To study the relative strength of two gas transitions in the most reliable way possible, the data cubes used to make the ratio maps need to be identical.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Regular circular rotation for the CO velocity gradient: rejected because the implied dynamical mass in the flat part of the PVD (~10^11 M_sun) is unrealistically large.

evidence.quote: However, if we assume that the observed velocity curves arise from gas in circular motions, the dynamical mass ($M_{\rm dyn} = \dfrac{v_{\rm rot}^{2}r}{G}$) in the “flat" part of the rotation curve would be $\approx10^{11}$ $M_{\odot}$, which is unrealistically large. We therefore conclude that the observed features do not trace regular circular rotation

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Single Gaussian spectral profile for CO(1-0) and CO(3-2): rejected via BIC test in favour of a two-Gaussian model (Delta BIC = 21.8 and 52.2).

evidence.quote: In both cases, the model with two Gaussians (overlaid as labelled in Figure 12) resulted as preferred and the evidence for the need of the second component as very strong, with $\Delta$BIC$= 21.8$ for the CO(1-0) and $\Delta$BIC$= 52.2$ for the CO(3-2).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Close binary nuclei as the origin of the two central optical compact residuals: rejected due to lack of spatial correlation with the optical peak, radio core, CO peaks, and ALMA continuum.

evidence.quote: We therefore conclude that it is unlikely that the two residual point-like structures in Figure 15 trace the presence of close binary nuclei.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Cavagnolo et al. (2010) scaling relation for estimating radio jet power: rejected because it yields an unrealistically high jet power (two orders of magnitude higher) and is unsuited to compact rapidly evolving radio sources.

evidence.quote: We note that using the well-known scaling relations of (cite: Cavagnolo10) results in an unrealistic jet power which is two orders of magnitude higher, and age correspondingly shorter – because this relation is not well-suited to compact radio sources which evolve rapidly through the size-luminosity space

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Supernovae or present-day AGN radiation pressure as the sole driver of the molecular outflow: rejected because estimated SNe mass outflow rate (68 M_sun/yr) and AGN radiation force (2.06e35 g cm s^-2) are too low.

evidence.quote: This excludes the power from supernovae as the main driver of the molecular outflow.
We thus conclude that the AGN radiation pressure is unlikely to be the only driver of the molecular outflow, at least at present times.

limitations_admitted.value: Gas kinematics is only mildly resolved, preventing a robust 3D kinematic modelling, and line-of-sight velocity dispersions (moment 2) can be significantly overestimated due to beam smearing.

evidence.quote: The moment 1 maps of the two CO transitions (Figure 7, middle panels) reveal that the gas kinematics is only mildly resolved at the resolution of all our observations. This prevents us from carrying out a robust kinematic modelling.

Among these, beam smearing (i.e. contamination from partially resolved velocity gradients within the host galaxy) is usually the dominant one, especially in regions of large velocity gradients and when the gas distribution is not fully resolved.

limitations_admitted.value: The synthesized beam of the smoothed line ratio cubes (0.42'' x 0.32'') is large compared to the complex gas sub-structures, impeding a fully spatially-resolved excitation analysis.

evidence.quote: As clearly illustrated by the Figure, the obtained beam size is quite large with respect to the size of the complex gas sub-structures, thus impeding a fully spatially-resolved analysis and inevitably leading us to miss the most reliable details on the gas physics.

limitations_admitted.value: Only single-band (i-band) optical VST photometry is available; multi-band colour (dust extinction) maps are needed to properly test the nuclear dust lane hypothesis for the compact residuals.

evidence.quote: However, colour (dust extinction) maps obtained from multi-band optical photometry would be needed to properly test this scenario and draw solid conclusions.

limitations_admitted.value: Both the radio source and dust distribution are unresolved in the ALMA continuum maps, preventing a morphological study of the continuum components.

evidence.quote: Both the radio source and the dust distribution are instead totally unresolved in all the ALMA continuum observations obtained so far (including those presented in this paper and illustrated in Figure 3), thus making difficult to carry out a morphological study that can corroborate the results obtained from the spectral analysis.

limitations_admitted.value: The GALMER simulation database has a narrow range of orbital parameters, lacks high resolution for complex gas physics, and does not include AGN feedback.

evidence.quote: For example, the range of orbital parameters explored in the database is narrow, the resolution of the GALMER simulations does not allow a thorough treatment of the complex gas physics, and no AGN feedback is included.

limitations_admitted.value: The high-resolution ALMA CO data resolve out the most extended part of the diffuse blueshifted outflow component detected in lower-resolution Cycle 0 data.

evidence.quote: At the higher-resolution of the CO data presented here, such blueshifted tail is much less extended in the 1-0 transition (while it is only barely detected in the 3-2), indicating that the most extreme part of this diffuse component is resolved out

referee_caveats_inferred: There is a discrepancy in the reported molecular gas mass between the Abstract ('(1.5 ± 0.3) x 10^10 M_sun') and Sections 3.3 / 6 ('(1.0 ± 0.1) x 10^10 M_sun'), likely a leftover value from Ruffa et al. (2018) in the abstract.
In Section 2.1, the Cycle 2 data are briefly referred to as 'Band 7' in the calibration paragraph ('manually calibrated the Cycle 2 (Band 7) data'), which is a typo for Band 6.

Outflow mass and energetics depend on an assumed ULIRG CO-to-H2 conversion factor (alpha_CO = 0.8); if the outflowing gas is optically thin and highly excited (as shown for CO(3-2)/CO(1-0) near the jet), alpha_CO could be lower, reducing M_out and M_dot_out.
Separating genuine outflowing gas from tidal merger debris/settling gas in an unrelaxed major merger without full kinematic modelling remains somewhat ambiguous.
